title: Ditching Annual Performance Reviews: The Adobe Story

The chapter matters because it moves away from annual-review logic and toward ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition around the work. That does not mean standards disappear. It means performance support becomes more useful while the work is still alive. A yearly review can summarize a period, but it is weaker than regular discussion that helps people adjust sooner. The case therefore treats continuous management as an operating change rather than as HR theater or soft encouragement.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The Adobe story matters because it turns Chapter 15's system into a company proof. The chapter argues that annual-review logic is too static to carry the full burden of performance management. Ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition are stronger because they help while the work is still moving. The point is not to erase accountability. The point is to change the cadence and usefulness of support around performance. Adobe therefore functions as the first named case showing that continuous performance management is an operational shift rather than HR theater.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Chapter 16 forces the Part 2 theory to survive inside a real company frame. chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The Adobe story matters because it is the first Part 2 company case after the transition into continuous performance management. Chapter 15 named the system. Chapter 16 asks whether that system can look practical inside a real company story rather than staying as a conceptual argument.

The chapter keeps its claim narrow. Annual-review logic is weaker when it has to carry too much of the performance burden by itself. A static yearly judgment can summarize a period, but it does not support the work especially well while the work is still moving. The Adobe case therefore shifts attention toward ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition.

That shift should not be mistaken for lower standards. The chapter does not replace accountability with positivity or a friendlier tone. Its stronger point is that performance support becomes more useful when discussion happens sooner, feedback arrives closer to the work, and recognition reinforces progress before the learning window closes.

This is why the case has to remain operational instead of rhetorical. If continuous management only changes the language around performance, then nothing important has improved. The case matters because it frames the move beyond annual reviews as a change in cadence and support quality rather than as HR theater.

The durable lesson is that continuous performance management becomes practical when a company depends less on static annual-review logic and more on useful ongoing support. Adobe therefore serves as the first company proof of the Part 2 system. Once that proof is clear, the book can move into another company story and test the same logic again from a different angle.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The Adobe story matters because it converts Chapter 15 from system language into a company proof. Part 2 has already argued for continuous performance management and CFRs. Chapter 16 now asks what that move looks like when a company stops relying so heavily on annual-review logic and shifts toward ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition around the work.

The chapter keeps one distinction sharp. A yearly review can still summarize a period, but it is too delayed and too static to carry the full burden of performance management by itself. Ongoing support is stronger because people can discuss performance, receive feedback, and adjust while the work is still alive instead of waiting for one large judgment later.

The chapter also protects a crucial limit. Leaving annual reviews behind does not mean lowering standards or removing accountability. The stronger system is not softer. It changes the cadence and usefulness of support so performance management becomes more operational and less trapped inside one formal ritual.

That is why the Adobe case must be read as an operating change rather than as HR rhetoric. The issue is not whether the company sounds more modern. The issue is whether conversation, feedback, and recognition become more central to how performance is actually supported.

The durable lesson is exact. Continuous performance management becomes practical when a company relies less on static annual-review logic and more on useful live support around performance. Adobe provides the first named company proof of that shift. The next chapter can then ask how another company story extends the same logic under a different pressure.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The Adobe story matters because Part 2 no longer gets to hide inside good theory. Chapter 15 defined the system. Chapter 16 now forces that system to survive inside a company case by challenging the old monopoly of annual-review logic.

The chapter keeps one line brutal and useful. A yearly verdict can summarize a period, but it is too blunt and too late to carry the whole performance burden by itself. That is why Adobe matters here. The case points toward ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition as stronger signals around the work while the work can still change.

The chapter also refuses a soft misreading. Leaving annual reviews behind is not code for easier standards, looser accountability, or friendlier language with no operating consequence. The stronger system is harder because support shows up earlier, stays more useful, and keeps performance discussion closer to the work itself.

This is why the case must stay operational. If continuous management only upgrades the vocabulary, the chapter collapses into HR theater. The Adobe story matters only if it proves that the cadence and quality of support have changed in a way that actually helps performance move.

So the lesson is severe. Continuous performance management becomes real when a company depends less on delayed ritual and more on live support around performance. Adobe is the first named proof that Part 2 can work under company conditions. The next case now has to show whether the same logic survives under another corporate pressure test.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: The Adobe story shows that moving beyond annual reviews means building more useful ongoing support around performance, not lowering standards.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Chapter 16 turns continuous performance management into a company proof by favoring live conversation, feedback, and recognition over annual-review logic alone.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Adobe matters because it breaks the delayed ritual's monopoly without going soft.
